start.topic: AniCheck: a mobile app for rice leaf disease identification

question.question: Regarding your decision to exclude diseases like sheath blight and false smut because they don't manifest on the leaves, how do you justify this limitation when it effectively narrows the utility of your tool for farmers facing these specific, common crop threats?

4. How acceptable is the developed application to its intended users when evaluated against the
ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics of functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability?
Objectives of the Study
The general objective was to develop and evaluate a mobile application capable of identifying
common rice leaf diseases without requiring an internet connection. Specifically, the study aimed to
assemble a labeled image dataset of rice leaves representing four disease classes and a healthy class;
to train a convolutional neural network on that dataset using transfer learning; to convert and embed
the trained model in an Android application with an interface suitable for users with limited formal
schooling; and to evaluate both the classification performance of the model and the acceptability of
the application to its intended users.
Scope and Limitations
The application identifies four disease classes — bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut, and
tungro — plus a healthy class. These four were selected because they were the diseases most
frequently named by farmers during the initial interviews and because they present visible foliar
symptoms. Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including
sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.
The image dataset was collected exclusively within Barangay Masagana during a six-week window
in the 2024 wet season. The application runs on Android 9.0 and above; no iOS version was
produced. The system returns an identification and a confidence percentage; it does not recommend
a specific chemical product or dosage, since the proponents judged that prescribing agricultural
chemicals falls outside both the competence of the development team and the intended function of a
diagnostic aid. The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for
consultation with a qualified agricultural technician.
Significance of the Study
For smallholder farmers, the study offers a means of obtaining a preliminary disease identification at
the moment of observation rather than at the next available consultation. For agricultural extension
officers, a tool that handles routine identification may allow scarce technician time to be directed
toward the cases that genuinely require expert judgment. For the local government unit, the
aggregate pattern of identifications could in principle inform the targeting of advisory campaigns,
although the present version of the system does not transmit or aggregate any data. For future
researchers, the study contributes a documented dataset collection procedure and a baseline set of
results against which alternative architectures may be compared.

question.grounding_reference: Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.

turns.answer: It does narrow the tool, and we chose that on purpose. Sheath blight shows mainly on the leaf sheath and stem, and false smut on the panicle, so a photo of a leaf can't diagnose either; including them would mean the app gives confident answers on symptoms its camera input never sees. We kept to the four foliar diseases the farmers named most often in our 24 interviews, bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut and tungro, plus healthy leaves, because their symptoms are on the leaf. The exclusion is stated in our Scope and Limitations, and extending coverage to stem and panicle diseases, which needs different images, is in our recommendations. Within its scope, the app answers the question farmers actually brought to a neighbor: what is this on my leaves.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate defends the scope via user-needs and technical constraints but does not address the practical risk of a user attempting to use the leaf-focused tool on panicle/stem symptoms regardless of the stated scope limitation.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate justifies excluding non-foliar diseases by citing the technical mismatch between camera input and symptom location, while noting that the chosen diseases were specifically identified as priorities by farmers.

Regarding your system acceptability survey, you had the proponents read each statement aloud and record the response; how do you justify this data collection method given the significant risk of social desirability bias when the survey administrator is also the researcher?

Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.
Responses were analyzed using weighted mean. The scale was interpreted according to the ranges in

Ethical Considerations
Permission to conduct the study within the barangay was obtained in writing from the barangay
captain. Participation was voluntary and respondents were informed that they could withdraw at any
point. Consent was obtained verbally at the start of each session, since several respondents indicated
discomfort with signing documents. No personally identifying information was recorded on the
survey forms, and the application stores identification history only on the user's own device.

turns.answer: We didn't isolate it, and I shouldn't have answered with belief. Reading the statements aloud was for respondents who were more comfortable listening than reading, but it means the proponents were present for every rating, right after a thirty-minute session they had guided, so acquiescence and a wish to please us could both push the means up. We have no control for it: no anonymous form, no independent administrator and no reverse-worded items. The one sign the respondents did discriminate is that the ratings weren't uniform: reliability came out lowest at 4.09, against 4.42 for usability, and it matches the model's real weakness on bacterial leaf blight. So I'd read the 4.31 overall as an upper bound on first-impression acceptability. The fix belongs with our longitudinal recommendation: an unsupervised season of use, rated on an anonymous instrument collected by someone outside the team.

evaluation.primary_gap: Acknowledgment of total lack of methodological controls for researcher-induced bias without pre-existing mitigation strategies.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate admitted that their methodology lacked controls for acquiescence bias and the Hawthorne effect due to the study design, reinterpreting their results as an upper-bound estimate rather than an absolute measure of acceptability.

next_question.question: That's a frank admission about the constraints of your single-class output. Given that you explicitly link the reliability-usability gap to the model's performance on bacterial leaf blight, why do you conclude that the system is useful when the users themselves expressed less confidence in the system's correctness than in its operation, especially when those users are making decisions based on potentially flawed single-class diagnostics?

Discussion
The overall accuracy of 94.7% is lower than the figures commonly reported in the plant disease
classification literature, where results above 99% on the PlantVillage dataset are routine. The
proponents attribute the difference principally to dataset scale: 3,240 images across five classes is an
order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.

turns.answer: Because we conclude it's useful for less than a diagnosis, and the respondents' doubt supports that narrower claim. Bacterial leaf blight has the lowest recall, 0.813: 16 of its 125 test images went to brown spot, since both start as yellowing along the leaf margin, while healthy leaves were almost never wrong at 0.994. So the realistic error is confusing a bacterial infection with a fungal one, and that's exactly why the app shows a confidence percentage and never a chemical or a dose. Reliability at 4.09, the only characteristic below Very Acceptable, tells us farmers shouldn't act on the result alone, and our conclusion says so: AniCheck is a preliminary identification aid that is easy to use offline, and it should not replace a technician where a costly treatment follows.

evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate argues the system is useful as a preliminary diagnostic aid rather than a definitive decision tool, citing the distinction between operational usability and clinical reliability as intentional by design.

next_question.question: I must push back on your reliance on 'farmer priorities' as a justification for excluding prevalent, non-foliar diseases, as your own Scope and Limitations section notes the system is meant to be a decision-support tool. If your design philosophy prioritizes user-identified needs, how can you claim this application provides genuine utility when you have deliberately omitted common threats like sheath blight, thereby forcing the farmer to distinguish between 'leaf-based' and 'non-foliar' symptoms before they even decide whether to open your app?

turns.answer: The farmer already makes that distinction, because it's where they look: a farmer who sees lesions on the leaf blade photographs the leaf, and one who sees rot at the base of the tiller or balls on the panicle is looking somewhere a leaf photo can't help. Our scope follows the symptom location, not only the interviews; the interviews told us which leaf diseases mattered most. Claiming utility for sheath blight would mean the model answering on images that don't show it, and a confident wrong answer there is worse than no answer. So the genuine utility is bounded: a fast, offline first identification for the four foliar diseases, with the limitation written into the Scope, and wider coverage, including stem and panicle images, listed as future work.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate fails to address the inherent conflict between defining a tool as 'decision-support' while simultaneously imposing a cognitive load on the user to pre-filter symptoms before interaction.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate argued that the system's utility is bounded by symptom location to avoid erroneous model predictions, asserting that farmers already distinguish between leaf and non-foliar symptoms based on observation.

report.narrative:
You have completed your defense, and the committee has reviewed your performance across several key areas. Overall, your presentation demonstrated strong clarity and grounding, with average scores of 80 and 84 respectively, indicating you communicated your core arguments well and stayed well-rooted in your evidence. Your depth of analysis averaged 64, which reflects the varying intensity of the questioning you encountered.

Your difficulty trajectory progressed from an initial level of 2 to a peak of 4 as the session unfolded. Notably, you demonstrated a strong capacity for recovery when the panel increased the pressure. During the pushback events at turns 2 and 3, where the difficulty escalated, your answer quality improved significantly at turn 2 and held steady at turn 3, showing you are capable of handling rigorous, high-difficulty inquiry.

However, the panel identified specific gaps that require your attention. Dr. O'Sullivan noted that you did not adequately address the risk of users misapplying your leaf-focused tool to stem or panicle symptoms. Dr. Nguyen raised concerns regarding social desirability bias and researcher-induced bias, noting that your response relied on subjective assumptions rather than experimental control. Additionally, Dr. Schmidt highlighted a conflict between your tool's status as decision-support and the cognitive load required for users to pre-filter symptoms. While your performance was marked by effective recovery under pressure, addressing these methodological and design-scope gaps will be essential to refining your final conclusions.

answer_suggestions.suggestion: A stronger answer would have explicitly acknowledged that sheath blight and false smut are indeed 'common crop threats' (as implied by the question) but immediately justified the exclusion by emphasizing that the design objective was specific to leaf-based symptoms, thereby making the tool useful for a specific, well-defined subset of common threats that can be diagnosed via leaf images, rather than claiming they aren't common.
answer_suggestions.grounding_reference: Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.

answer_suggestions.suggestion: A stronger answer would have immediately acknowledged the significant risk of social desirability bias inherent in the method, rather than dismissing it with an assumption about farmer honesty. It should then have stated any procedural steps taken, however minimal, to try and mitigate this risk, or explicitly stated it as a limitation of the study.
answer_suggestions.grounding_reference: the survey was administered immediately afterward, with the proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.

answer_suggestions.suggestion: A stronger answer, while already quite comprehensive, could have more explicitly linked the observed variability in ratings (e.g., reliability at 4.09 vs. usability at 4.42) to the verbal interpretations provided in Table 2 (e.g., 'Acceptable' vs. 'Very Acceptable'), to further contextualize how even within a potentially biased dataset, meaningful distinctions were still observed, thus strengthening the argument that respondents did discriminate.

answer_suggestions.suggestion: A stronger answer would have reiterated the overall positive acceptability (e.g., stating the overall acceptability or that usability was 'Very Acceptable'), while emphasizing that the specific area of lower confidence (reliability rated 'Acceptable') precisely informed the carefully circumscribed conclusion of the system's utility as a 'preliminary identification aid' and not a replacement for experts.
answer_suggestions.grounding_reference: The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them.

answer_suggestions.suggestion: A stronger answer would have explicitly referenced the tool's classification as a 'decision-support tool' (as stated in the chunk_text) and argued that its genuine utility, though bounded, is precisely in providing focused decision support for foliar diseases that can be diagnosed from leaf images, thereby guiding farmers who have already identified leaf-based symptoms to the correct next step.
answer_suggestions.grounding_reference: The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for consultation with a qualified agricultural technician.

order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.

transcript.grounding_reference: respondents were more confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.
transcript.answer: Because we conclude it's useful for less than a diagnosis, and the respondents' doubt supports that narrower claim. Bacterial leaf blight has the lowest recall, 0.813: 16 of its 125 test images went to brown spot, since both start as yellowing along the leaf margin, while healthy leaves were almost never wrong at 0.994. So the realistic error is confusing a bacterial infection with a fungal one, and that's exactly why the app shows a confidence percentage and never a chemical or a dose. Reliability at 4.09, the only characteristic below Very Acceptable, tells us farmers shouldn't act on the result alone, and our conclusion says so: AniCheck is a preliminary identification aid that is easy to use offline, and it should not replace a technician where a costly treatment follows.

evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate argues the system is useful as a preliminary diagnostic aid rather than a definitive decision tool, citing the distinction between operational usability and clinical reliability as intentional by design.

closing.line: I will leave it at that regarding the limitations of your diagnostic framework.

transcript.question: I must push back on your reliance on 'farmer priorities' as a justification for excluding prevalent, non-foliar diseases, as your own Scope and Limitations section notes the system is meant to be a decision-support tool. If your design philosophy prioritizes user-identified needs, how can you claim this application provides genuine utility when you have deliberately omitted common threats like sheath blight, thereby forcing the farmer to distinguish between 'leaf-based' and 'non-foliar' symptoms before they even decide whether to open your app?

3. What level of classification accuracy does the trained convolutional neural network achieve on a
held-out test set?
4. How acceptable is the developed application to its intended users when evaluated against the
ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics of functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability?
Objectives of the Study
The general objective was to develop and evaluate a mobile application capable of identifying
common rice leaf diseases without requiring an internet connection. Specifically, the study aimed to
assemble a labeled image dataset of rice leaves representing four disease classes and a healthy class;
to train a convolutional neural network on that dataset using transfer learning; to convert and embed
the trained model in an Android application with an interface suitable for users with limited formal
schooling; and to evaluate both the classification performance of the model and the acceptability of
the application to its intended users.
Scope and Limitations
The application identifies four disease classes — bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut, and
tungro — plus a healthy class. These four were selected because they were the diseases most
frequently named by farmers during the initial interviews and because they present visible foliar
symptoms. Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including
sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.
The image dataset was collected exclusively within Barangay Masagana during a six-week window
in the 2024 wet season. The application runs on Android 9.0 and above; no iOS version was
produced. The system returns an identification and a confidence percentage; it does not recommend
a specific chemical product or dosage, since the proponents judged that prescribing agricultural
chemicals falls outside both the competence of the development team and the intended function of a
diagnostic aid. The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for
consultation with a qualified agricultural technician.
Significance of the Study
For smallholder farmers, the study offers a means of obtaining a preliminary disease identification at
the moment of observation rather than at the next available consultation. For agricultural extension
officers, a tool that handles routine identification may allow scarce technician time to be directed
toward the cases that genuinely require expert judgment. For the local government unit, the
aggregate pattern of identifications could in principle inform the targeting of advisory campaigns,
although the present version of the system does not transmit or aggregate any data. For future
researchers, the study contributes a documented dataset collection procedure and a baseline set of
results against which alternative architectures may be compared.

transcript.grounding_reference: Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.
transcript.answer: The farmer already makes that distinction, because it's where they look: a farmer who sees lesions on the leaf blade photographs the leaf, and one who sees rot at the base of the tiller or balls on the panicle is looking somewhere a leaf photo can't help. Our scope follows the symptom location, not only the interviews; the interviews told us which leaf diseases mattered most. Claiming utility for sheath blight would mean the model answering on images that don't show it, and a confident wrong answer there is worse than no answer. So the genuine utility is bounded: a fast, offline first identification for the four foliar diseases, with the limitation written into the Scope, and wider coverage, including stem and panicle images, listed as future work.

evaluation.primary_gap: The candidate fails to address the inherent conflict between defining a tool as 'decision-support' while simultaneously imposing a cognitive load on the user to pre-filter symptoms before interaction.
evaluation.answer_summary: The candidate argued that the system's utility is bounded by symptom location to avoid erroneous model predictions, asserting that farmers already distinguish between leaf and non-foliar symptoms based on observation.
